speaker: NARRATOR
text: The last day before Christmas had passed. A clear winter night had come. The stars looked out. The moon rose majestically into the sky to shed light on good people and on the whole world, so that everyone might have a merry time singing carols and praising Christ. The frost was sharper than in the morning, but it was so still that the creak of the frost under a boot could be heard half a mile away. Not one crowd of lads had yet appeared under the windows of the cottages; only the moon peeped into them, stealthily, as if calling the girls who were dressing up to run out quickly onto the creaking snow. Then smoke came tumbling in clouds out of the chimney of one cottage and spread like a storm cloud across the sky, and with the smoke a witch rose up, riding on a broom.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: If at that moment the Sorochintsy assessor had been driving by in a troika of requisitioned horses, in a cap with a lambskin band cut in the lancer fashion, in a blue sheepskin coat lined with black astrakhan, with the devilishly plaited whip he is accustomed to use on his driver, he would certainly have noticed her, because no witch in the world can slip past the Sorochintsy assessor. He knows to the last piglet how many a woman's sow has farrowed, and how much linen lies in her chest, and exactly which of his clothes and belongings a good man will pawn at the tavern on Sunday. But the Sorochintsy assessor was not driving by, and why should he care about other people's affairs? He has his own district.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Meanwhile the witch rose so high that she showed only as a little black speck up there. But wherever the speck appeared, the stars vanished from the sky, one after another. Soon the witch had gathered a whole sleeveful of them. Three or four were still shining. Suddenly, from the other side, another speck appeared, grew bigger, began to stretch out, and was a speck no longer. A short-sighted man, even if he put the wheels of a commissary's carriage on his nose instead of spectacles, would not have made out what it was. In front he was a perfect German: a narrow little muzzle, forever turning and sniffing at everything that came its way, ended, like our pigs', in a round little snout; his legs were so thin that if the Yareski headman had had such legs he would have broken them in the first Cossack dance. But behind he was a real provincial attorney in uniform, because a tail hung from him, as sharp and long as the tails of a uniform coat nowadays; only by the goat's beard under his muzzle, by the little horns sticking out of his head, and by being no whiter than a chimney sweep could one guess that he was neither a German nor a provincial attorney, but simply a devil, who had one last night left to wander the wide world and teach good people their sins.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Tomorrow, at the first bells for morning service, he would run without looking back, tail between his legs, to his lair.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Meanwhile the devil crept quietly up to the moon and had already stretched out his hand to seize it; but suddenly he snatched it back, as if burned, sucked his fingers, jigged about on one foot, ran round to the other side, and again jumped away and drew back his hand. Still, in spite of all his failures, the cunning devil did not give up his mischief. He ran up and suddenly grabbed the moon with both hands, and, grimacing and blowing, tossed it from one hand to the other, like a peasant who has picked up a live coal with his bare hands to light his pipe; at last he hurriedly hid it in his pocket and, as if nothing had happened, ran on. In Dikanka no one heard how the devil stole the moon. True, the district clerk, coming out of the tavern on all fours, saw the moon dancing in the sky for no reason at all, and swore to the whole village that it was so; but the villagers shook their heads and even laughed at him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And what was the reason that made the devil decide on such a lawless deed? This was the reason: he knew that the rich Cossack Chub had been invited by the deacon to the Christmas Eve supper of kutya, where the headman would be; and the deacon's kinsman, who had come from the bishop's choir, in a blue frock coat, singing the lowest bass; and the Cossack Svyerbyhuz and a few others; where, besides the kutya, there would be varenukha, vodka brewed with saffron, and plenty of other good things to eat. Meanwhile Chub's daughter, the beauty of the whole village, would stay at home, and to the daughter the blacksmith would surely come, a strong man and a fine fellow, whom the devil hated worse than the sermons of Father Kondrat. In his spare time from his work the blacksmith took up painting, and was known as the best painter in all the neighbourhood.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Colonel L...ko himself, who was still alive then, sent for him specially to Poltava to paint the board fence round his house. All the bowls from which the Dikanka Cossacks ate their borscht had been painted by the blacksmith. The blacksmith was a God-fearing man and often painted icons of the saints, and even now you can find his Evangelist Luke in the church at T... But the triumph of his art was a picture painted on the church wall in the right-hand porch, in which he had shown Saint Peter on the Day of Judgement, with the keys in his hands, driving the evil spirit out of hell: the frightened devil threw himself in every direction, sensing his doom, while the sinners who had been shut up there before beat and drove him with whips, logs and anything that came to hand. While the painter was working on this picture, painting it on a large wooden board, the devil tried with all his might to hinder him: he jogged his arm unseen, lifted ashes from the forge's furnace and sprinkled them over the picture; but in spite of everything the work was finished, the board was carried into the church and set into the wall of the porch, and from that time the devil swore to take revenge on the blacksmith.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He had only one night left to wander the world; but even on this night he was looking for some way to pay the blacksmith back for his spite. And for that he decided to steal the moon, hoping that old Chub was lazy and slow to get going, and that the deacon's house was not close to his cottage: the road ran behind the village, past the windmills, past the cemetery, and wound round a ravine. Even on a moonlit night the varenukha and the vodka brewed with saffron might have lured Chub; but in such darkness it would hardly have been possible for anyone to drag him off his stove and out of his cottage. And the blacksmith, who had long been on bad terms with him, would never dare, with Chub there, to go to the daughter, strong as he was. And so, as soon as the devil had hidden his moon in his pocket, it suddenly became so dark all over the world that not everyone could have found the way to the tavern, let alone to the deacon's.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The witch, finding herself suddenly in the dark, cried out. Then the devil, sidling up like a little imp, took her by the arm and began whispering in her ear the very thing that is usually whispered to the whole female race. A strange arrangement we have in this world! Everything that lives in it tries to copy and mimic everything else. Once upon a time, in Mirgorod, only the judge and the mayor went about in winter in sheepskin coats covered with cloth, while all the petty officials wore plain bare ones; but now the assessor and the chamberlain have both had new fur coats made from Reshetilovka lambskin with cloth covers. The clerk and the district scribe, the year before last, bought blue Chinese cotton at sixty kopecks an arshin. The sexton has made himself nankeen trousers for summer and a waistcoat of striped cloth. In a word, everyone is climbing up in the world!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: When will these people stop being vain? One could wager that many will find it surprising to see the devil setting off down the same road. What is most annoying is that he surely imagines himself a handsome fellow, while his figure is a shame to look at. A face, as Foma Grigoryevich says, the ugliest of the ugly, and yet even he courts the ladies! But in the sky and under the sky it had become so dark that it was no longer possible to see what happened next between them.

speaker: CHUB
text: “So you, friend, have not been to the deacon's new cottage yet?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Cossack Chub, coming out of the door of his cottage, to a lean, tall peasant in a short sheepskin coat, with an overgrown beard, which showed that for more than two weeks it had not been touched by the bit of scythe blade with which peasants usually shave for want of a razor.

speaker: CHUB
text: “There'll be a fine drinking party there now,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub went on, his face breaking into a grin.

speaker: CHUB
text: “If only we are not late.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: With this Chub straightened his belt, which held his sheepskin coat tight, pulled his cap down more firmly, gripped in his hand his whip, the terror and scourge of pestering dogs, and then, glancing upward, stopped short.

speaker: CHUB
text: “What the devil! Look! Look, Panas!”

speaker: PANAS
text: “What?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said his friend, and lifted his head, looking up too.

speaker: CHUB
text: “What do you mean, what? There's no moon!”

speaker: PANAS
text: “What the plague! There really is no moon.”

speaker: CHUB
text: “That's just it, there isn't,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, with some annoyance at his friend's unfailing calm.

speaker: CHUB
text: “You, I dare say, don't care.”

speaker: PANAS
text: “What am I to do about it!”

speaker: CHUB
text: “It had to be some devil,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub went on, wiping his moustache with his sleeve,

speaker: CHUB
text: “may that dog never get a glass of vodka in the morning, to meddle in this! Really, as if to mock us. I sat in the cottage on purpose and looked out of the window: the night was a marvel! Bright; the snow shone in the moonlight. You could see everything as in the day. I had hardly stepped out of the door when, look, you can't see your hand before your face!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub went on grumbling and swearing for a long time, and meanwhile was wondering what to decide. He was dying to chat about all sorts of nonsense at the deacon's, where without a doubt the headman was already sitting, and the visiting bass, and Mykyta the tar-seller, who drove to Poltava every fortnight to the markets and let fly such jokes that all the villagers held their sides with laughter. Chub could already see in his mind the varenukha standing on the table. All this was tempting, it was true; but the darkness of the night reminded him of that laziness which is so dear to every Cossack. How good it would be now to lie with his legs tucked under him on the stove-bench, calmly smoking his pipe, and through a blissful drowsiness listen to the carols and songs of the merry lads and girls crowding in bunches under the windows.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Without a doubt he would have decided on the latter if he had been alone; but now, with two of them, it was not so dull or frightening to go in the dark night, and he also did not want to appear lazy or cowardly in front of others. When he had finished his curses, he turned again to his friend.

speaker: CHUB
text: “So there's no moon, friend?”

speaker: PANAS
text: “No.”

speaker: CHUB
text: “Strange, really. And give me a pinch of snuff! You've got famous snuff, friend! Where do you get it?”

speaker: PANAS
text: “Famous, what the devil!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered his friend, closing his birch snuffbox, pricked all over with patterns.

speaker: PANAS
text: “An old hen wouldn't sneeze at it!”

speaker: CHUB
text: “I remember,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub went on in the same tone,

speaker: CHUB
text: “the late tavern-keeper Zuzulya once brought me tobacco from Nezhin. Ah, that was tobacco! Good tobacco! Well, friend, what shall we do? It's dark out.”

speaker: PANAS
text: “Then perhaps we should stay at home,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said his friend, taking hold of the door handle.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: If his friend had not said that, Chub would surely have decided to stay; but now something seemed to be pulling him to go against him.

speaker: CHUB
text: “No, friend, let's go! We can't not, we must go!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: No sooner had he said this than he was annoyed with himself for saying it. It was most unpleasant to him to trudge out on such a night; but it consoled him that he had wanted it himself, on purpose, and had done as he pleased and not as he had been advised.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The friend, without showing the slightest trace of annoyance on his face, like a man to whom it is quite the same whether he sits at home or trudges out of it, looked about, scratched his shoulders with the stick of his whip, and the two friends set off.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now let us see what the beautiful daughter is doing, left alone. Oksana was not yet seventeen, and all over the world, one might say, on this side of Dikanka and on that, there was talk of nothing but her. The lads declared in chorus that there had never yet been a better girl in the village, and never would be. Oksana knew and heard everything that was said about her, and was capricious, as a beauty is. If she had gone about not in a plakhta and a zapaska but in some kind of fine town gown, she would have driven away all her girl friends. Lads chased after her in crowds, but, losing patience, they left her little by little and turned to others who were not so spoiled. Only the blacksmith was stubborn and did not give up his courting, although he too was treated no better than the rest. After her father had gone out, she went on dressing up and primping for a long time before a small mirror in a pewter frame, and could not admire herself enough.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “What have people taken it into their heads to spread about, that I am pretty?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: she said, as if absent-mindedly, only to have something to chatter about with herself.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “People lie, I am not pretty at all.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But the fresh, lively face that flashed in the mirror, young as a child's, with shining black eyes and an inexpressibly pleasant smile that burned into the soul, suddenly proved the opposite.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Are my black brows and eyes,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the beauty went on, not letting go of the mirror,

speaker: OKSANA
text: “so lovely that there is nothing like them in the world? What is good about this turned-up nose? And these cheeks? And these lips? Are my black braids lovely, then? Oh! They could frighten you in the evening: like long snakes, they are twisted and wound around my head. I see now that I am not pretty at all!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, holding the mirror a little farther from her, she cried out:

speaker: OKSANA
text: “No, I am pretty! Oh, how pretty! A wonder! What joy I shall bring to him whose wife I become! How my husband will admire me! He won't remember himself. He will kiss me to death!”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “A strange girl!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: whispered the blacksmith, who had come in quietly.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “And she isn't short of boasting! She has been standing an hour looking in the mirror, and cannot look enough, and even praises herself aloud!”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Yes, lads, are you a match for me? Look at me,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the pretty coquette went on,

speaker: OKSANA
text: “how smoothly I walk; my shift is sewn with red silk. And what ribbons on my head! You will never see richer braid! My father bought me all this so that the finest young man in the world would marry me!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, smiling, she turned the other way, and saw the blacksmith...

speaker: NARRATOR
text: She cried out and stopped sternly in front of him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith let his arms drop.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It is hard to say what the dark-skinned face of the wonderful girl expressed: there was sternness in it, and through the sternness some mockery of the confused blacksmith, and a barely noticeable flush of vexation spread delicately over her face; and all this was so mingled and so indescribably lovely that to kiss her a million times was the best thing anyone could have done then.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Why have you come here?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Oksana began.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Do you want me to drive you out of the door with a shovel? You are all masters at getting round us. You sniff out in a moment when our fathers are not at home. Oh, I know you! Well, is my chest ready?”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “It will be ready, my little heart, it will be ready after the holiday. If you knew how much I have slaved over it: two nights I did not leave the forge; but not one priest's daughter will have such a chest. I put on it iron for the binding such as I did not put on the colonel's cart when I went to work in Poltava. And how it will be painted! Though you walk the whole district on your little white feet, you will not find one like it! Red and blue flowers will be scattered all over the field. It will burn like fire. Don't be angry with me! Let me at least talk, at least look at you!”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Who forbids you? Talk and look!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: She sat down on the bench and again looked in the mirror, and began to set her braids straight on her head. She looked at her neck, at her new shift embroidered with silk, and a delicate feeling of self-satisfaction showed on her lips, on her fresh cheeks, and shone in her eyes.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Let me sit beside you, too!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Sit,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana, keeping the same feeling on her lips and in her contented eyes.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Wonderful, dearest Oksana, let me kiss you!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the emboldened blacksmith, and pressed her to him, meaning to snatch a kiss; but Oksana turned away her cheeks, which were already at an imperceptible distance from the blacksmith's lips, and pushed him off.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “What more do you want? When he has honey, he needs a spoon too! Go away, your hands are harder than iron. And you smell of smoke yourself. I think you have smeared me all over with soot.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then she held up the mirror and began to preen before it again.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “She doesn't love me!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith thought to himself, hanging his head.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “To her it is all a game; and I stand before her like a fool and can't take my eyes off her. And I would go on standing before her, and never take my eyes off her! A wonderful girl! What would I not give to know what is in her heart, whom she loves. But no, she does not care about anyone. She admires herself; she torments me, poor man; and for sorrow I can't see the light; and I love her as no man in the world has loved, or ever will love.”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Is it true that your mother is a witch?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana, and laughed; and the blacksmith felt that everything inside him laughed. That laughter seemed at once to echo in his heart and in his gently trembling veins, and yet vexation sank into his soul that it was not in his power to kiss that face which had laughed so sweetly.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What do I care about my mother? You are mother to me, and father, and everything that is dear in the world. If the tsar called me and said: Blacksmith Vakula, ask of me whatever is best in my kingdom, and I will give it to you. I shall order a golden forge to be made for you, and you will forge with silver hammers. I don't want, I would say to the tsar, neither precious stones, nor a golden forge, nor all your kingdom: give me rather my Oksana!”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “See what you are! But my father is no fool himself. You will see whether he marries your mother!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana, smiling slyly.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “But the girls are not coming... What can it mean? It is high time to go carolling. I am getting bored.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “God be with them, my beauty!”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Not likely! The lads will surely come with them. Then the fun begins. I can imagine what funny stories they will tell!”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “So you have a good time with them?”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Yes, better than with you. Ah! Someone knocked; it must be the girls with the lads.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What more is there to wait for?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith said to himself.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “She is mocking me. To her I am as dear as a rusted horseshoe. But if so, then at least no one else will get to laugh at me. Let me only see for certain who pleases her more than I do; I will cure him...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A knock at the door and a voice ringing sharply in the frost, “Open!”, interrupted his thoughts.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Wait, I will open it myself,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, and went out into the passage, meaning in his vexation to break the ribs of the first man he met.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The frost grew stronger, and up there it became so cold that the devil hopped from one little hoof to the other and blew into his fist, trying to warm his freezing hands a little. No wonder, though, that he should freeze, who had been knocking about from morning to morning in hell, where, as is well known, it is not so cold as with us in winter, and where, putting on a cook's cap and standing before the hearth like a real chef, he roasted sinners with the pleasure with which a housewife usually fries sausage at Christmas. The witch herself felt it was cold, although she was warmly dressed; and so, raising her arms, thrusting out one leg, and putting herself in the position of a man flying on skates, without moving a single joint she slid down through the air as down a slippery icy slope, straight into the chimney.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The devil followed her in the same manner. But since this creature is nimbler than any dandy in stockings, it is no wonder that at the very entrance to the chimney he ran into his sweetheart's neck, and both found themselves in the roomy stove among the pots. The traveller quietly pushed back the stove door to look and see whether her son Vakula had invited guests into the cottage, but seeing that there was no one, except the sacks lying in the middle of the room, she climbed out of the stove, threw off her warm sheepskin, tidied herself, and no one could have known that a minute before she had been riding a broom. The mother of the blacksmith Vakula was no more than forty years old. She was neither pretty nor plain. It is hard to be pretty at such an age. Yet she knew how to charm the most respectable Cossacks (who, it does no harm to remark, cared little for beauty), so that the headman used to visit her, and the deacon Osip Nikiforovich (of course, if the deacon's wife was not at home), and the Cossack Korniy Chub, and the Cossack Kasyan Svyerbyhuz.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, to her credit, she knew how to deal with them skilfully. It never entered the head of any of them that he had a rival. Whether a pious peasant, or a gentleman, as the Cossacks call themselves, dressed in a cloak with a hood, was going on Sunday to church, or, if the weather was bad, to the tavern, how could he not drop in on Solokha, eat the rich dumplings with sour cream, and chat in a warm cottage with the talkative, obliging hostess? And the gentleman would make a big detour on purpose before reaching the tavern, and call it dropping in on the way. And when Solokha went to church on a holiday, in a bright plakhta with a Chinese-cotton zapaska and over it a blue skirt with gold whiskers sewn on the back, and stood right by the right-hand choir, the deacon would surely begin to cough and involuntarily screw up his eyes in that direction; the headman would stroke his moustache, wind his forelock round his ear and say to the neighbour standing near him: “Ah, a fine woman!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A devil of a woman!” Solokha bowed to each of them, and each thought she bowed to him alone.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But anyone fond of meddling in other people's business would have noticed at once that Solokha was friendliest of all to the Cossack Chub. Chub was a widower; eight stacks of grain always stood before his cottage. Two pairs of sturdy oxen always thrust their heads out of the wattled shed into the street and lowed when they saw the cow, their friend, passing, or Uncle, the fat bull. A bearded goat climbed right up on the roof and bleated from there in a harsh voice, like a mayor, teasing the turkeys that strutted about the yard, and turning his back when he saw his enemies, the boys who made fun of his beard. In Chub's chests there was plenty of linen, coats, and old-fashioned kuntushes with gold braid: his late wife had been a fashionable woman. In the vegetable garden, besides poppies, cabbages and sunflowers, two fields of tobacco were sown every year.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: All this Solokha thought it no bad thing to add to her own household, considering beforehand what order it would take when it passed into her hands, and she doubled her kindness to old Chub. And so that her son Vakula might not somehow get at his daughter and manage to take everything himself, in which case he would certainly not let her meddle in anything, she resorted to the usual means of all forty-year-old gossips: to set Chub and the blacksmith at odds as often as possible. Perhaps it was these very tricks and her shrewdness that were the cause of old women beginning here and there to say, especially when they had drunk a drop too much at some merry gathering, that Solokha really was a witch; that the lad Kizyakolupenko had seen a tail on her behind no bigger than a woman's spindle; that only the Thursday before last she had run across the road as a black cat; that once a pig had run to the priest's wife, crowed like a cock, put Father Kondrat's hat on its head and run back.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It happened that while the old women were discussing this, the cowherd Tymish Korostyavy came along. He did not fail to tell how in summer, just before Saint Peter's day, when he had lain down to sleep in the cattle shed with straw under his head, he had seen with his own eyes a witch with her hair loose, in her shift alone, begin to milk the cows, and he could not stir, so bewitched was he; when she had milked the cows, she came to him and smeared his lips with something so foul that he spat for a whole day afterwards. But all this is somewhat doubtful, because only the Sorochintsy assessor can see a witch. And so all the distinguished Cossacks waved their hands when they heard such talk. “They are lying, the bitches!” was their usual answer.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: When she had climbed out of the stove and tidied herself, Solokha, like a good housewife, began to clear up and put everything in its place; but she did not touch the sacks: Vakula had brought them, so let him carry them out himself! The devil meanwhile, as he flew into the chimney, happened to turn round and saw Chub arm in arm with his friend, already far from the cottage. In a moment he flew out of the stove, ran across their path, and began to tear up the heaps of frozen snow on all sides. A blizzard rose. The air turned white. The snow whirled back and forth like a net and threatened to plaster the eyes, mouth and ears of the walkers. And the devil flew back into the chimney, firmly convinced that Chub would turn back with his friend, find the blacksmith, and give him such a welcome that for a long time he would be unable to take a brush in his hand and paint insulting caricatures.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In fact, no sooner had the blizzard risen and the wind begun to cut straight into his eyes than Chub declared his regret and, pulling his cap lower on his head, treated himself, the devil and his friend to curses. However, this annoyance was feigned. Chub was very glad of the blizzard. To the deacon's there was still eight times as much distance as they had covered. The travellers turned back. The wind blew on the back of their heads; but through the sweeping snow nothing could be seen.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Stop, friend! I think we are not going the right way,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, after going a little distance.

speaker: CHUB
text: “I don't see a single cottage. Ugh, what a blizzard! Turn a little to the side, friend, perhaps you will find the road; and in the meantime I will look here. The unclean spirit must have driven us to trudge about in such a storm! Don't forget to shout when you find the road. Ugh, what a heap of snow Satan has thrown in my eyes!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The road, however, was nowhere to be seen. The friend, moving off to the side, wandered back and forth in his long boots and at last came straight upon the tavern. This find so delighted him that he forgot everything and, shaking off the snow, went into the porch, not troubling himself in the least about his friend left in the street. To Chub meanwhile it seemed that he had found the road; stopping, he began to shout at the top of his voice, but seeing that his friend did not appear, he decided to go on alone. After going a little way he saw his cottage. Drifts of snow lay around it and on the roof. Clapping his hands, numb with cold, he began to knock at the door and shout, in a commanding voice, to his daughter to open it.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What do you want here?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the blacksmith, coming out, sternly.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub, recognising the blacksmith's voice, stepped back a little.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Ah, no, this is not my cottage,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said to himself,

speaker: CHUB
text: “the blacksmith would not stray into my cottage. And then, if one looks carefully, it is not the blacksmith's either. Whose cottage could it be? There now! I didn't recognise it! This is lame Levchenko's, who has lately married a young wife. His is the only cottage like mine. That is why it seemed a little strange to me at first that I had come home so quickly. But Levchenko is sitting at the deacon's now, I know that; so why is the blacksmith here? Aha, ha, ha! He is visiting his young wife. So that's how it is! Good! Now I understand it all.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Who are you, and why are you hanging about at the door?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, more sternly than before, coming closer.

speaker: CHUB
text: “No, I won't tell him who I am,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought Chub.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Heaven knows, the accursed brute may even thrash me!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, changing his voice, he answered:

speaker: CHUB
text: “It is I, a good man, who have come to sing carols a little under your windows, for your amusement.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Go to the devil with your carols!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted Vakula angrily.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Why are you standing there? Do you hear, get out of here this minute!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub himself already had this sensible intention; but it seemed annoying to him to be forced to obey the blacksmith's orders. It seemed that some evil spirit jogged his arm and forced him to say something contrary.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Why are you really shouting so?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said in the same voice.

speaker: CHUB
text: “I want to sing carols, and that's all.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Aha! You won't stop at words!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: With these words Chub felt a very painful blow on the shoulder.

speaker: CHUB
text: “So you are beginning to fight, I see!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, backing away a little.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Go, go!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the blacksmith, rewarding Chub with another shove.

speaker: CHUB
text: “What are you doing!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, in a voice that expressed pain, and annoyance, and timidity.

speaker: CHUB
text: “You are not fighting in jest, I see, and you hit hard, too!”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Go, go!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the blacksmith and slammed the door.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Look how brave he has become!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, left alone in the street.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Just try to come near! Look at him! What a great fine fellow! You think I won't find justice against you. No, my dear, I will go, and go straight to the commissary. You will learn from me. I won't look at your being a blacksmith and a painter. But let me look at my back and shoulders: I think there are blue marks. He must have beaten me hard, the enemy's son! A pity it is cold and I don't want to take off my sheepskin! Just wait, you devilish blacksmith, may the devil beat you and your forge, you will dance for this! Look at the accursed rascal! But then, he is not at home now. Solokha, I think, is sitting alone. Hm... it is not far from here; I might go! It is the sort of time that no one will catch us. Perhaps it will even be possible to... look how hard he beat me, the accursed blacksmith!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here Chub, scratching his back, set off in another direction. The pleasure awaiting him ahead in his meeting with Solokha eased the pain a little and made him insensible even to the frost, which crackled in all the streets, unmuffled by the whistling of the blizzard. From time to time on his face, whose beard and moustache the storm had lathered with snow more quickly than any barber who tyrannically seizes his victim by the nose, a half-sweet expression appeared. But if the snow had not been crossing and recrossing everything before his eyes, one could have seen for a long time how Chub stopped, scratched his back, said, “He beat me hard, the accursed blacksmith!” and set off on his way again.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At the time when the nimble dandy with the tail and goat's beard was flying out of the chimney and then back into the chimney, the pouch that hung at his side on a strap, into which he had hidden the stolen moon, somehow happened to catch in the stove and came open, and the moon, taking advantage of the chance, flew out through the chimney of Solokha's cottage and rose smoothly into the sky. Everything was lit up. The blizzard was gone as if it had never been. The snow blazed into a wide silver field and was all sprinkled with crystal stars. The frost seemed to grow warmer. Crowds of lads and girls appeared with sacks. Songs rang out, and there was scarcely a cottage under whose windows carollers were not crowding. How wonderfully the moon shines! It is hard to tell how good it is to knock about, on such a night, among a crowd of laughing, singing girls and among lads ready for any joke and invention that a merrily laughing night can inspire.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Under a thick sheepskin it is warm; the frost makes the cheeks burn even brighter; and for mischief the sly one himself pushes you from behind. Crowds of girls with sacks burst into Chub's cottage and surrounded Oksana. Shouts, laughter, stories deafened the blacksmith. They all vied in hurrying to tell the beauty something new, unloaded their sacks and boasted of the loaves, sausages and dumplings which they had already managed to collect in plenty for their carols. Oksana seemed to be in perfect pleasure and joy, chattered now with one, now with another, and laughed without stopping. With a sort of vexation and envy the blacksmith looked at such merriment and, this time, cursed the carols, although he himself was usually mad about them.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Ah, Odarka!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the merry beauty, turning to one of the girls.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “You have new shoes! Oh, how pretty! And with gold! It is good for you, Odarka, you have a man who buys you everything; and I have no one to get such lovely shoes for me.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Don't grieve, my dearest Oksana!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith broke in.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I will get you such shoes as few young ladies wear.”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “You?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana, glancing quickly and haughtily at him.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “I shall see where you will get shoes that I could put on my foot. Unless you bring me the very ones the Empress wears.”

speaker: GIRLS
text: “Look what she has asked for!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the crowd of girls, laughing.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Yes!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the beauty went on proudly.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Be witnesses, all of you: if the blacksmith Vakula brings me the very shoes the Empress wears, then here is my word that I will marry him that very hour.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The girls led the capricious beauty away with them.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Laugh, laugh!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, going out after them.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I laugh at myself! I think and cannot think where my wits have gone. She does not love me, well, God be with her! As if there were only one Oksana in all the world. Thank God, there are plenty of good girls in the village without her. And what is Oksana? She will never make a good housewife; she is only a master at dressing up. No, enough, it is time to stop playing the fool.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But at the very moment when the blacksmith was preparing to be resolute, some evil spirit carried before him the laughing image of Oksana, saying mockingly:

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Get me the Empress's shoes, blacksmith, and I will marry you!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Everything in him was stirred, and he thought of Oksana alone.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Crowds of carollers, the lads by themselves, the girls by themselves, hurried from one street to another. But the blacksmith walked and saw nothing and took no part in the merriment that he had once loved more than anyone.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The devil meanwhile had grown seriously tender at Solokha's: he kissed her hand with the grimaces of an assessor before a priest's daughter, clutched his heart, groaned, and said plainly that if she would not agree to satisfy his passion and reward him, as is the custom, he was ready for anything, would throw himself into the water, and send his soul straight to the pit. Solokha was not so cruel; besides, the devil, as is well known, was working on her side. She did like to see a crowd dragging after her and was seldom without company; this evening, however, she had thought to spend alone, because all the distinguished inhabitants of the village had been invited to the deacon's for kutya. But everything went otherwise: the devil had barely put forward his demand when suddenly the voice of the stout Headman was heard. Solokha ran to open the door, and the nimble devil climbed into a sack that was lying there.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Headman, shaking the snow from his cap and drinking a glass of vodka from Solokha's hand, told her that he had not gone to the deacon's because a blizzard had risen; and seeing a light in her cottage, he had turned in with the intention of spending the evening with her. He had hardly said this when there was a knock at the door and the deacon's voice.

speaker: HEAD
text: “Hide me somewhere,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: whispered the Headman.

speaker: HEAD
text: “I don't want to meet the deacon now.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Solokha thought a long time where to hide such a solid guest; at last she chose the biggest sack of coal; she poured the coal into a tub, and the stout Headman climbed into the sack, with his moustache, his head and his cap.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The deacon came in, coughing and rubbing his hands, and told her that no one had come to his house, and that he was heartily glad of this chance to spend a little time at her place, and had not been afraid of the blizzard. Then he came closer to her, coughed, smiled, touched her bare, plump arm with his long fingers, and said, with a look that showed both slyness and self-satisfaction:

speaker: DEACON
text: “And what is this you have here, magnificent Solokha?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And having said this, he jumped back a little.

speaker: SOLOKHA
text: “What do you mean, what? An arm, Osip Nikiforovich!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered Solokha.

speaker: DEACON
text: “Hm! An arm! Heh, heh, heh!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the deacon, heartily pleased with his beginning, and walked about the room.

speaker: DEACON
text: “And what is this you have here, most precious Solokha?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, with the same look, approaching her again and lightly seizing her neck with his hand, and in the same manner jumping back.

speaker: SOLOKHA
text: “As if you can't see, Osip Nikiforovich!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered Solokha.

speaker: SOLOKHA
text: “A neck, and on the neck a string of beads.”

speaker: DEACON
text: “Hm! On the neck a string of beads! Heh, heh, heh!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the deacon again walked about the room, rubbing his hands.

speaker: DEACON
text: “And what is this you have here, incomparable Solokha?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It is not known what the deacon would now have touched with his long fingers, when suddenly a knock came at the door and the voice of the Cossack Chub.

speaker: DEACON
text: “Ah, my God, an outsider!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the deacon in fright.

speaker: DEACON
text: “What if they find a person of my calling here? It will reach Father Kondrat!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But the deacon's fears were of another kind: he was more afraid that his better half would find out, who with her terrible hand had already turned his thick pigtail into the very thinnest.

speaker: DEACON
text: “For God's sake, virtuous Solokha,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, trembling all over,

speaker: DEACON
text: “your kindness, as the Gospel of Luke says, chapter thir... thir... They are knocking, by God, knocking! Oh, hide me somewhere!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Solokha poured the coal from another sack into the tub, and the deacon, not too bulky in body, climbed into it and sat right at the bottom, so that another half sack of coal could have been poured on top of him.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Good evening, Solokha!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, coming into the cottage.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Perhaps you did not expect me, eh? True, you did not expect me? Perhaps I have interrupted you...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub went on, putting on his face a merry and significant look, which gave notice beforehand that his slow head had been working and was preparing to deliver some sharp and clever joke.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Perhaps you were amusing yourselves here with someone! Perhaps you have already hidden somebody, eh?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, delighted with this remark of his, Chub laughed, inwardly triumphing that he alone enjoyed Solokha's favour.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Well, Solokha, give me some vodka now. I think my throat has frozen from the accursed frost. God sent such a night before Christmas! How it took hold, you hear, Solokha, how it took hold... ugh, how my hands have gone stiff: I can't unbutton my sheepskin! How the blizzard took hold...”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Open!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: a voice rang out in the street, accompanied by a thump on the door.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Somebody is knocking?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, stopping short.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Open!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: they shouted, louder than before.

speaker: CHUB
text: “It is the blacksmith!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, clutching his cap.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Listen, Solokha, put me wherever you like; for nothing in the world will I show myself to that accursed brute, may a blister as big as a haystack rise under each of his eyes, the devil's son!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Solokha, frightened herself, rushed about like one in a daze and, forgetting herself, signed to Chub to climb into the very sack in which the deacon was already sitting. The poor deacon did not dare even to show his pain by a cough or a groan when the heavy peasant sat almost on his head and placed his boots, frozen from the frost, on both sides of his temples.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith came in without saying a word, without taking off his cap, and almost fell onto the bench. It was plain that he was in a very bad mood. Just as Solokha was shutting the door behind him, someone knocked again. It was the Cossack Svyerbyhuz. This one could no longer be hidden in a sack, because no such sack could be found. He was heavier in body than the Headman himself, and taller than Chub's friend. And so Solokha led him out into the vegetable garden, to hear from him everything he wanted to tell her.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith looked absently into the corners of his cottage, listening from time to time to the songs of the carollers carrying far off; at last he rested his eyes on the sacks.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Why are these sacks lying here? They should have been taken away long ago. Because of this stupid love I have gone quite silly. Tomorrow is a holiday, and all kinds of rubbish are still lying in the cottage. Take them to the forge!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: With that the blacksmith bent down to the huge sacks, tied them tighter and prepared to heave them onto his shoulders. But it was plain that his thoughts were wandering God knows where, or else he would have heard how Chub hissed when the rope tying the sack twisted the hair on his head, and the stout Headman began to hiccup quite audibly.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Will that wretched Oksana never get out of my mind?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I don't want to think of her; yet I keep thinking, and as if on purpose, of her alone. Why is it that a thought forces itself into the head against one's will? What the devil, the sacks seem to have grown heavier than before! Something besides coal must have been put in here. Fool that I am! I forgot that now everything seems heavier to me. Once upon a time I could bend and straighten a copper coin and a horseshoe in one hand; and now I can't lift sacks of coal. Soon I shall be falling over in the wind. No,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he cried, after a pause, taking heart,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “what sort of woman am I! I won't let anyone laugh at me. Even ten such sacks, I will lift them all.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And he briskly heaved onto his shoulders the sacks that two stout men could not have carried.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Take this one too,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he went on, lifting the little one, at the bottom of which the devil lay curled up.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I think I put my tools in here.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Saying this, he went out of the cottage, whistling a song:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I'll have no bother with a wife.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Songs and shouts rang out ever louder in the streets. The crowds of jostling people were swelled still more by those who came from the neighbouring villages. The lads played pranks and ran wild to their heart's content. Often among the carols one heard some merry song which one of the young Cossacks had just made up on the spot. Then suddenly one of the crowd, instead of a carol, would let fly a shchedrovka and roar at the top of his voice:

speaker: NARRATOR
text: “Shchedryk, vedryk! Give us a dumpling! A little lump of porridge, a ring of sausage!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Laughter rewarded the joker. Little windows were raised, and the lean hand of an old woman (they alone, with the staid fathers, stayed in the cottages) was thrust out of the window with a sausage in it or a piece of pie. The lads and girls vied in holding out their sacks and catching their booty. In one place the lads, coming up from all sides, surrounded a crowd of girls: noise, shouting, one threw a snowball, another snatched a sack full of all sorts of things. In another place the girls caught a lad, tripped him, and he flew headlong to the ground together with his sack. It seemed they were ready to make merry all night long. And the night, as if on purpose, glowed so luxuriously! and the light of the moon seemed still whiter from the glitter of the snow. The blacksmith stopped with his sacks. In the crowd of girls he fancied he heard Oksana's voice and thin laughter. Every little vein in him trembled; throwing the sacks on the ground, so that the deacon at the bottom groaned from the bump and the Headman hiccuped at the top of his voice, he trudged with the small sack on his shoulders after the crowd of lads who were following the girls' crowd, among whom he had heard Oksana's voice.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Yes: it is she! She stands like a queen, and her black eyes flash! A fine lad is telling her something; surely something funny, because she is laughing. But she is always laughing. As if involuntarily, not understanding himself how, the blacksmith pushed through the crowd and stood beside her.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Ah, Vakula, you are here! Good evening!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the beauty with the very same smile that nearly drove Vakula out of his mind.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Well, have you collected much? Oh, what a small sack! And the shoes the Empress wears, have you got them? Get me the shoes and I will marry you!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, laughing, she ran off with the crowd.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith stood rooted to the spot.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “No, I can't; I have no more strength...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said at last.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “But, my God, why is she so devilishly beautiful? Her look, and her words, and everything, it just burns and burns... No, I cannot master myself any longer! It is time to put an end to everything: let my soul perish, I will go and drown myself in the ice-hole, and goodbye!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then with a resolute step he went forward, overtook the crowd, drew level with Oksana, and said in a firm voice:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Farewell, Oksana! Find yourself whatever husband you like, fool whom you like; but you will not see me any more in this world.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The beauty seemed surprised, wanted to say something, but the blacksmith waved his hand and ran off.

speaker: LADS
text: “Where to, Vakula?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the lads, seeing the blacksmith run.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Farewell, brothers!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the blacksmith in reply.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “God willing, we shall meet in the next world; but in this one we shall not make merry together any more. Farewell, do not think ill of me! Tell Father Kondrat to say a requiem for my sinful soul. I have not painted the candles for the icons of the Wonder-Worker and the Mother of God, I am sinful, being busy with worldly affairs. All the goods that are found in my chest, for the church! Farewell!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Having said this, the blacksmith began to run again with the sack on his back.

speaker: LADS
text: “He has gone out of his mind!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the lads.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “A lost soul!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: an old woman passing by muttered piously.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “I will go and tell how the blacksmith hanged himself!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Vakula meanwhile, having run several streets, stopped to catch his breath.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Where am I really running to?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he thought.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “As if everything were already lost. I will try one more way: I will go to the Zaporozhian, Pot-bellied Patsyuk. They say he knows all the devils and will do whatever he wants. I will go, for my soul will have to be lost anyway!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At this the devil, who had lain a long time without any movement, began to jump for joy in the sack; but the blacksmith, thinking that he had somehow caught the sack with his hand and made the movement himself, struck the sack with his stout fist and, shaking it on his shoulders, set off to Pot-bellied Patsyuk.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: This Pot-bellied Patsyuk had indeed once been a Zaporozhian; but whether they had driven him out or he had himself run away from the Zaporozhian Host, no one knew. It was long since, ten years, perhaps fifteen, that he had lived in Dikanka. At first he lived like a true Zaporozhian: he did no work, slept three quarters of the day, ate for six mowers, and drank almost a whole pail at one time; though there was room for it, because Patsyuk, for all his small height, was quite hefty in breadth. Besides, the trousers he wore were so wide that however big a step he took, his legs could not be seen at all, and it seemed as if a distillery vat were moving down the street. Perhaps this very thing gave rise to his nickname, Pot-bellied. Only a few days had passed after his arrival in the village when everyone already knew that he was a healer.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: If anyone was ill with anything, they at once called Patsyuk; and all Patsyuk had to do was whisper a few words, and the ailment was removed as if by hand. If it happened that a hungry gentleman choked on a fishbone, Patsyuk knew how to strike him on the back with his fist so skilfully that the bone went where it ought, causing no harm to the gentleman's throat. Lately he was rarely seen anywhere. The reason for this was perhaps laziness, perhaps also that squeezing through doors became harder for him every year. Then the villagers had to go to him themselves if they had need of him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith, not without timidity, opened the door and saw Patsyuk sitting on the floor, Turkish fashion, in front of a small tub on which stood a bowl of dumplings. This bowl stood, as if on purpose, level with his mouth. Without moving a single finger he bent his head slightly to the bowl and slurped the broth, catching the dumplings now and then with his teeth.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “No, this one,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought Vakula to himself,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “is even lazier than Chub: Chub at least eats with a spoon; and this one won't even lift a hand!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Patsyuk was surely deeply occupied with the dumplings, for he seemed not to have noticed the blacksmith's arrival at all, and the blacksmith, hardly setting foot on the threshold, gave him a very low bow.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I have come to your honour, Patsyuk!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Vakula, bowing again. The fat Patsyuk raised his head and began again to slurp his dumplings.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “They say, no offence meant,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, gathering his courage,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I say this not to cause you any insult, that you are somewhat related to the devil.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Having said these words, Vakula was frightened, thinking that he had still spoken too plainly and had softened the strong words too little, and expecting that Patsyuk, seizing the tub together with the bowl, would send it straight at his head, he drew back a little and covered himself with his sleeve so that the hot broth from the dumplings would not splash his face.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But Patsyuk glanced at him and began again to slurp his dumplings.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Encouraged, the blacksmith decided to go on:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I have come to you, Patsyuk, may God give you everything, all good things in plenty, bread in proportion!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith sometimes knew how to slip in a fashionable word; he had become practised in that while still in Poltava, when he was painting the colonel's board fence.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I am to be lost, sinner that I am! Nothing helps in the world! Come what may, I must ask for help from the devil himself. Well, Patsyuk?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, seeing his unchanging silence.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What am I to do?”

speaker: PATSYUK
text: “When you need the devil, go to the devil!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered Patsyuk, not raising his eyes to him and going on clearing away the dumplings.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “That is why I have come to you,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the blacksmith, making a bow,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I think no one in the world but you knows the way to him.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Patsyuk said not a word, and finished the last dumplings.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Do me the kindness, good man, do not refuse!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith pressed on.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Pork, or sausages, buckwheat flour, well, linen, millet, or anything else in case of need... as is usual among good people... we will not be stingy; only tell me how, let us say, to get on the road to him?”

speaker: PATSYUK
text: “He need not go far who has the devil at his back,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Patsyuk indifferently, without changing his position.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Vakula fixed his eyes on him as if the explanation of these words were written on his forehead. What is he saying? his look asked silently; and his half-open mouth was ready to swallow the first word like a dumpling. But Patsyuk was silent. Then Vakula noticed that neither dumplings nor tub were before him; instead there stood on the floor two wooden bowls: one was filled with vareniki, the other with sour cream. His thoughts and eyes turned involuntarily to these dishes.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Let us see,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said to himself,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “how Patsyuk will eat the vareniki. He surely will not want to bend down to slurp them as he did the dumplings, and it is not possible: a varenik must first be dipped in the sour cream.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He had hardly had time to think this when Patsyuk opened his mouth, looked at the vareniki, and opened his mouth wider. At that moment a varenik splashed out of the bowl, plopped into the sour cream, turned over on the other side, leaped up, and landed right in his mouth. Patsyuk ate it and opened his mouth again, and a varenik went the same way again. He took upon himself only the work of chewing and swallowing.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Look, what a marvel!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought the blacksmith, opening his mouth in amazement, and at that very moment noticed that a varenik was climbing into his mouth too and had already smeared his lips with sour cream. Pushing the varenik away and wiping his lips, the blacksmith began to reflect on what wonders there are in the world and what wisdom the unclean spirit can lead a man to, noting at the same time that only Patsyuk could help him.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I will bow to him once more, let him explain it properly... But what the devil! Today is the fasting kutya; and he is eating vareniki, meat-day vareniki! What sort of fool am I, really: standing here and gathering sin! Back!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the pious blacksmith ran headlong out of the cottage.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But the devil, who sat in the sack and had been rejoicing beforehand, could not bear that such a fine prey should escape his hands. As soon as the blacksmith put down the sack, he jumped out of it and sat astride his neck.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A chill ran over the blacksmith's skin; frightened and pale, he did not know what to do, and already wanted to cross himself... But the devil, bending his doggy little snout to his right ear, said:

speaker: DEVIL
text: “It is I, your friend; I will do everything for a comrade and friend! I will give you as much money as you like,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he squeaked into his left ear.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Oksana will be ours today,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he whispered, turning his muzzle again to the right ear. The blacksmith stood thinking.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Very well,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said at last,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “for such a price I am ready to be yours!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The devil clapped his hands and began to gallop with joy on the blacksmith's neck.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Now the blacksmith is caught!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he thought to himself.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Now I will pay you back, my dear, for all your paintings and the tall tales told about devils! What will my comrades say now when they learn that the most pious man in the whole village is in my hands?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here the devil laughed for joy, remembering how he would tease the whole tailed tribe in hell, how the lame devil, considered the first among them for inventions, would rage.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Well, Vakula!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: squeaked the devil, still not getting down from his neck, as if afraid that he would run away.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “You know that nothing is done without a contract.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I am ready!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I hear that with you they sign in blood; wait, I will get a nail out of my pocket!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here he put his hand behind him, and grab! he had the devil by the tail.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Look what a joker!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the devil, laughing.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Well, enough, enough of this mischief!”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Wait, my dear!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “And how does this strike you?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At these words he made the sign of the cross, and the devil became as quiet as a lamb.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Wait, then,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, dragging him down to the ground by the tail,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “you will learn from me to prompt good people and honest Christians to sin.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then the blacksmith, without letting go of the tail, leaped astride him and raised his hand for the sign of the cross.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Have mercy, Vakula!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: groaned the devil pitifully.

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Everything you need, I will do; only let my soul go to repentance: do not lay the terrible cross on me!”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Ah, so that is the voice you sing in, accursed German! Now I know what to do. Carry me on yourself this very instant! Do you hear, carry me like a bird!”

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Where?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the sorrowful devil.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “To Petersburg, straight to the Empress!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the blacksmith went numb with fear, feeling himself rise into the air.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Oksana stood a long time, pondering the blacksmith's strange words. Already something inside her told her that she had treated him too cruelly.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “What if he really decides on something terrible? Heaven knows! Perhaps in his grief he will take it into his head to fall in love with another and out of spite will call her the first beauty in the village? But no, he loves me. I am so pretty! He will not exchange me for anything; he is playing, pretending. Not ten minutes will pass before he surely comes to look at me. I really am harsh. I must let him kiss me, as if unwillingly. How glad he will be!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the flighty beauty was already joking with her friends.

speaker: GIRLS
text: “Wait,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said one of them,

speaker: GIRLS
text: “the blacksmith has forgotten his sacks; look: what terrible sacks! He did not carol as we do: I think they have thrown a whole quarter of a ram into them; and the sausages and loaves surely cannot be counted. Luxury! You could gorge on them for whole holidays.”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Are these the blacksmith's sacks?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Oksana caught up.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Let us drag them quickly to my cottage and look properly at what he has packed in here.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: All approved this proposal with laughter.

speaker: GIRLS
text: “But we can't lift them!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the whole crowd cried at once, trying to move the sacks.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Wait,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana,

speaker: OKSANA
text: “let us run quickly for a sledge and take them on the sledge!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And the crowd ran for a sledge.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The prisoners were greatly tired of sitting in the sacks, although the deacon had poked a fair hole for himself with his finger. If there had been no people about, he might have found a means of climbing out; but to climb out of the sack before everyone, to show himself to be laughed at... this held him back, and he decided to wait, only coughing a little under Chub's impolite boots. Chub himself wished no less for freedom, feeling that under him lay something on which it was terribly uncomfortable to sit. But as soon as he heard his daughter's decision he calmed down and no longer wanted to climb out, reasoning that to reach his cottage he had to go at least a hundred paces, perhaps two hundred. And once out, he would have to tidy himself, button his sheepskin, tie his belt: so much work! and besides, his cap had been left at Solokha's.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Better let the girls bring him on the sledge. But it turned out quite differently from what Chub expected: at the time the girls ran for the sledge, the lean friend was coming out of the tavern, upset and out of sorts. The tavern-keeper would not on any account trust him with credit; he had meant to wait in case some pious gentleman came and treated him; but, as if on purpose, all the gentlemen stayed at home and, as honest Christians, were eating kutya in the midst of their families. Reflecting on the corruption of manners and on the wooden heart of the Jewess who sold wine, the friend came upon the sacks and stopped in astonishment.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Look what sacks someone has thrown down in the road!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, looking about on all sides.

speaker: PANAS
text: “There must be pork here, too. Somebody was lucky to collect so many things by carolling. What terrible sacks! Suppose they are stuffed only with buckwheat cakes and flat cakes, even that is good. Even if there were only loaves here, that would be tasty: the Jewess gives a glass of vodka for each loaf. Drag them off quickly, so that no one sees.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then he heaved onto his shoulders the sack with Chub and the deacon, but felt that it was too heavy.

speaker: PANAS
text: “No, it will be hard to carry alone,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said,

speaker: PANAS
text: “but here, as if on purpose, comes the weaver Shapuvalenko. Good evening, Ostap!”

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Good evening,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver, stopping.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Where are you going?”

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Oh, just walking where my feet take me.”

speaker: PANAS
text: “Help me carry the sacks, good man! Someone was carolling and threw them down in the middle of the road. We will share them in friendship, half and half.”

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Sacks? And what is in the sacks, rolls or loaves?”

speaker: PANAS
text: “I think there is everything.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then they quickly pulled some sticks out of a wattle fence, laid the sack on them, and carried it on their shoulders.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Where shall we carry it? To the tavern?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: asked the weaver on the way.

speaker: PANAS
text: “I thought so myself, to the tavern; but the accursed Jewess will not believe it, she will even think we stole it somewhere; besides, I have only just come from the tavern. We will carry it to my cottage. No one will disturb us: my wife is not at home.”

speaker: WEAVER
text: “But is she really not at home?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: asked the careful weaver.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Thank God, we are not quite out of our wits yet,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Would the devil bring me where she is? She will drag about with the women till daylight, I think.”

speaker: WIFE
text: “Who is there?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the friend's wife, hearing the noise in the porch made by the arrival of the two companions with the sack, and opening the door.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The friend stood rooted to the spot.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Well, there you are!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver, letting his arms fall.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The friend's wife was the sort of treasure of which there are not a few in the world. Like her husband she almost never sat at home and crawled about almost the whole day among her gossips and well-to-do old women, praising and eating with great appetite, and fought only in the mornings with her husband, because only at that time did she sometimes see him. Their cottage was twice as old as the district clerk's trousers: in some places the roof had no thatch. Of the fence only remnants were visible, because everyone who left the house never took a stick for the dogs, in the hope that he would pass the friend's vegetable garden and pull one out of his fence. The stove was not lit for days at a time. Everything the tender wife begged from good people she hid as far as possible from her husband, and often forcibly took away his booty if he had not managed to drink it away at the tavern. The friend, in spite of his constant coolness, did not like to give way to her; and so he almost always left the house with lanterns under both eyes, and his dear half, groaning, trailed off to tell the old women about her husband's outrages and the beatings she had suffered from him.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now one can imagine how the weaver and the friend were taken aback by such an unexpected appearance. Putting down the sack, they stood in front of it and covered it with the skirts of their coats; but it was too late: the friend's wife, although she saw badly with her old eyes, noticed the sack all the same.

speaker: WIFE
text: “That is good!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: she said with a look in which the joy of a hawk could be seen.

speaker: WIFE
text: “It is good that you have collected so much by carolling! That is how good people always do; but no, I think you have picked it up somewhere. Show me at once, do you hear, show me your sack this minute!”

speaker: PANAS
text: “The bald devil will show you, not we,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend, drawing himself up.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “What business is it of yours?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “We collected it, not you.”

speaker: WIFE
text: “No, you will show me, worthless drunkard!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the wife, striking the tall friend with her fist on the chin and pushing through to the sack. But the weaver and the friend bravely defended the sack and made her fall back. They had hardly recovered when the wife ran out into the porch, already with a poker in her hands. Quickly she struck her husband on the hands with the poker, the weaver on the back, and was already standing beside the sack.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Why did we let her in?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver, coming to his senses.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Oh, why did we let her! And why did you let her!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend coolly.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Your poker must be iron!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver after a short silence, scratching his back.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “My wife bought a poker last year at the fair; gave half a kopeck for it; and that one is nothing... it doesn't hurt...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Meanwhile the triumphant wife, setting a little lamp on the floor, untied the sack and looked into it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But surely her old eyes, which had seen the sack so well, were deceived this time.

speaker: WIFE
text: “Oh, there is a whole boar lying here!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: she cried, clapping her hands with joy.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “A boar! Do you hear, a whole boar!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the weaver nudged his friend.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “And it is all your fault!”

speaker: PANAS
text: “What is to be done!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend, shrugging his shoulders.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “What do you mean, what? Why are we standing here? Let us take the sack away! Come on, attack!”

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Get away! Away! This is our boar!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: shouted the weaver, stepping forward.

speaker: PANAS
text: “Go, go, you devil's woman! This is not your property!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend, coming closer.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The wife took up the poker again, but at that moment Chub climbed out of the sack and stood in the middle of the porch, stretching like a man who had just woken from a long sleep.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The friend's wife cried out, striking her hands against her skirts, and everyone involuntarily gaped.

speaker: PANAS
text: “What is she saying, the fool: a boar! This is not a boar!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the friend, goggling.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Look what a man has been thrown into the sack!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver, backing away in fright.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Say what you like, burst if you will, but there is the unclean power in this. He would not even fit through the window!”

speaker: PANAS
text: “It is friend Chub!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the friend, looking closer.

speaker: CHUB
text: “And who did you think it was?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, smiling.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Well, what a fine trick I played on you! And you, I dare say, wanted to eat me instead of pork? Wait, then, I will please you: there is something else in the sack, if not a boar then surely a piglet or some other creature. Something was moving under me all the time.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The weaver and the friend rushed to the sack, the lady of the house seized it from the opposite side, and the fight would have broken out again if the deacon, seeing now that he had nowhere to hide, had not scrambled out of the sack.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The friend's wife, rooted to the spot, let go of the leg by which she had begun to pull the deacon out of the sack.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “Here is another one!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the weaver in fear.

speaker: WEAVER
text: “The devil knows how things are in the world... my head is spinning... not sausages and loaves, but people are thrown into sacks!”

speaker: CHUB
text: “It is the deacon!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, more astonished than anyone.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Well, there you are! Good for Solokha! To put him in a sack... So that is why I saw her cottage full of sacks... Now I know everything: she had two men sitting in every sack. And I thought she had only me... well, there is Solokha for you!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The girls were a little surprised at not finding one sack.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Nothing to be done, this one will do for us,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: babbled Oksana. All took hold of the sack and heaved it onto the sledge. The Headman resolved to keep silent, reasoning that if he shouted to be let out and the sack untied, the foolish girls would run away and think that the devil was sitting in the sack, and he would be left in the street, perhaps till tomorrow. The girls meanwhile, joining hands in a friendly way, flew like a whirlwind with the sledge over the creaking snow. A crowd of them, playing about, sat on the sledge; others climbed onto the Headman himself. The Headman resolved to bear everything.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At last they arrived, threw wide the door in the porch and the cottage, and with laughter dragged in the sack.

speaker: GIRLS
text: “Let us see what is lying here,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: they all cried, rushing to untie it. Then the hiccups, which had not ceased to torment the Headman the whole time he sat in the sack, grew so strong that he began to hiccup and cough at the top of his voice.

speaker: GIRLS
text: “Oh, there is someone sitting in there!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: they all cried, and in fright rushed out of the door.

speaker: CHUB
text: “What the devil! Where are you rushing off to, like mad things?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, coming in at the door.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Oh, father!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “There is someone sitting in the sack!”

speaker: CHUB
text: “In the sack? Where did you get this sack?”

speaker: GIRLS
text: “The blacksmith threw it down in the middle of the road,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: they all said at once.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Well, so, did I not say...?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought Chub to himself.

speaker: CHUB
text: “What are you frightened of? Let us see: come now, my good man, I beg you not to be angry that we do not call you by name and patronymic, climb out of the sack!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Headman climbed out.

speaker: GIRLS
text: “Ah!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the girls.

speaker: CHUB
text: “And the Headman has got in there too,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub said to himself in bewilderment, measuring him from head to foot.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Look at that!... Eh!...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: More than this he could not say.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Headman himself was no less embarrassed and did not know what to begin.

speaker: HEAD
text: “It must be cold outside?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he said, turning to Chub.

speaker: CHUB
text: “There is a bit of frost,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered Chub,

speaker: CHUB
text: “and allow me to ask you, what do you grease your boots with, lard or tar?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: He did not mean to say this; he meant to ask: how did you, Headman, get into this sack; but he himself did not understand how he had said something quite different.

speaker: HEAD
text: “Tar is better,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Headman.

speaker: HEAD
text: “Well, farewell, Chub!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, pulling his cap down, he left the cottage.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Why did I ask, like a fool, what he greases his boots with!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Chub, glancing at the door by which the Headman had gone out.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Good for Solokha! To stuff a man like that into a sack!... Look at her, the devil's woman! And I am a fool... but where is that accursed sack?”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “I threw it in the corner, there is nothing more in it,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Oksana.

speaker: CHUB
text: “I know these tricks, nothing in it! Hand it here: there is another one sitting in there! Shake it well... What, no?... Look at her, the accursed woman! And to look at her, a saint, as if she had never put anything but Lenten food in her mouth.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But let us leave Chub to pour out his vexation at leisure, and return to the blacksmith, for it must surely be nine o'clock outside by now.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At first it seemed terrifying to Vakula when he rose from the earth to such a height that he could see nothing below, and flew like a fly right under the moon, so that if he had not bent down a little he would have caught it with his cap. But a little later he took heart and began to make fun of the devil.
