It amused him beyond measure how the devil sneezed and coughed when he took the cypress-wood cross from his neck and held it out to him. On purpose he would lift his hand to scratch his head, and the devil, thinking he was about to be crossed, flew still faster. Everything was bright up on high. The air, in a light silver mist, was transparent. Everything could be seen, and one could even notice how a sorcerer swept past them like a whirlwind, sitting in a pot; how the stars, gathered in a heap, played blind man's buff; how a whole swarm of spirits swirled to one side like a cloud; how a devil, dancing in the moonlight, took off his cap when he saw the blacksmith riding along on horseback; how a broom came flying back, on which a witch had evidently just ridden where she was needed... they met much more such rubbish.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: All of them, seeing the blacksmith, stopped for a minute to look at him and then rushed on again and went about their business; the blacksmith flew on, and suddenly Petersburg blazed up before him, all in fire. (There was an illumination at the time, for some occasion.) The devil, flying over the barrier, turned into a horse, and the blacksmith saw himself on a spirited trotter in the middle of the street. My God!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Clatter, thunder, glitter; on both sides four-storey walls loomed; the horse's hooves and the sound of the wheels echoed like thunder and rang back from four sides; houses grew and seemed to rise out of the earth at every step; bridges trembled; carriages flew; cabmen and postilions shouted; the snow whistled under a thousand sledges flying from every side; pedestrians huddled and crowded under houses strung with lamps, and their enormous shadows flickered along the walls, reaching the chimneys and roofs with their heads. In amazement the blacksmith looked around on all sides. It seemed to him that all the houses had fixed on him their countless fiery eyes and were watching. Gentlemen in cloth-covered fur coats he saw so many that he did not know to whom to take off his cap.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “My God, how many gentry there are here!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I think everyone who walks down the street in a fur coat is an assessor, an assessor! And those who ride in such wonderful glass-windowed carriages, if they are not mayors, then surely commissaries, and perhaps even more.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: His words were interrupted by the devil's question:

speaker: DEVIL
text: “Shall we go straight to the Empress?”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “No, it is frightening,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Somewhere here, I don't know where, the Zaporozhians who passed through Dikanka in the autumn are lodging. They were travelling from the Sich with papers for the Empress; all the same I should consult them. Hey, Satan, climb into my pocket, and lead me to the Zaporozhians!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In one minute the devil grew thin and became so small that he climbed into his pocket without difficulty.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And Vakula had no time to look round before he found himself in front of a big house, went, not knowing how, up the stairs, opened the door, and drew back a little from the glitter at the sight of a splendidly furnished room; but he took heart a little, recognising the very Zaporozhians who had passed through Dikanka, sitting on silk sofas, with their tarred boots tucked under them, smoking the strongest tobacco, usually called roots.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Good health to you, gentlemen! God help you! So this is where we meet!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith, coming close and bowing to the ground.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “What man is that?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: asked one who sat right in front of the blacksmith, of another who sat farther off.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “And you do not recognise me?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “It is I, Vakula the blacksmith! When you passed through Dikanka in the autumn, you stayed, God give you every health and long life, nearly two days. And I put a new tire on the front wheel of your wagon then!”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Ah!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the same Zaporozhian.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “It is that blacksmith who paints so grandly. Hello, countryman! What has God brought you here for?”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Oh, just wanted to have a look, they say...”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Well, countryman,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Zaporozhian, drawing himself up and wishing to show that he too could speak in Russian.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Vot, a beeg city?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith did not want to disgrace himself and appear a novice either; besides, as we have had occasion to see above, he knew the learned language himself.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “A notable province!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he answered indifferently.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Nothing to say, the houses are enormous, important paintings hang everywhere. Many houses are inscribed with letters of gold leaf, to the extreme. Nothing to say, a marvellous proportion!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Zaporozhians, hearing the blacksmith express himself so freely, drew a conclusion very advantageous to him.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “We will talk with you more later, countryman; now we are going at once to the Empress.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “To the Empress? Be so kind, gentlemen, take me with you!”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “You?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Zaporozhian, with the look with which a nurse speaks to her four-year-old charge who asks to be put on a real, big horse.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “What will you do there? No, it is not possible.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At this a significant expression appeared on his face.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “We, brother, shall be talking with the Empress about our own affairs.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Take me!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: insisted the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Ask!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he whispered quietly to the devil, striking his pocket with his fist. He had hardly said this when another Zaporozhian said:

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Let us take him, really, brothers!”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Let us take him, then!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the others.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Put on clothes like ours.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith hastened to pull on a green coat, when suddenly the door opened and a man with gold lace came in and said it was time to go.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It seemed strange to the blacksmith again when he rushed along in an enormous carriage, swaying on its springs, when on both sides four-storey houses ran backwards past him and the pavement, thundering, seemed to roll itself under the horses' feet.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “My God, what a light!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: thought the blacksmith to himself.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “With us it is never so bright by day.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The carriages stopped in front of a palace. The Zaporozhians got out, entered a magnificent hall, and began to climb a brilliantly lit staircase.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What a staircase!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: whispered the blacksmith to himself.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “It is a pity to tread on it with one's feet. What decorations! They say fairy tales lie; what the devil do they lie! My God, what banisters! What workmanship! Fifty roubles' worth of iron alone went into this!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Having climbed the stairs, the Zaporozhians passed through the first hall. The blacksmith followed them timidly, fearing at every step to slip on the parquet. They passed through three halls, and the blacksmith did not cease to marvel.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Entering the fourth, he involuntarily went up to a picture that hung on the wall. It was the Most Pure Virgin with the Child in her arms.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “What a picture! What wonderful painting!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he reflected.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Look, it seems to speak! It seems alive! And the Holy Child! And he has pressed his little hands! And smiles, poor thing! And the colours! My God, what colours! There is not a kopeck's worth of ochre here, I think, all verdigris and crimson. And the blue fairly burns! A grand piece of work! The ground must have been laid with white lead. But however wonderful these paintings are, this copper handle,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he went on, going up to the door and feeling the lock,

speaker: VAKULA
text: “deserves still greater wonder. What clean workmanship! All this, I think, was made by German blacksmiths at the dearest prices...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Perhaps the blacksmith would have gone on reasoning a long time if a footman with braid had not jogged his arm and reminded him not to fall behind the others. The Zaporozhians passed through two more halls and stopped. Here they were told to wait.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: In the hall a number of generals crowded, in gold-embroidered uniforms. The Zaporozhians bowed on all sides and stood in a heap. A minute later there came in, accompanied by a whole retinue, a rather stout man of majestic height, in a hetman's uniform, in yellow boots. His hair was dishevelled, one eye slightly squinting, on his face there was a kind of haughty grandeur, and in all his movements the habit of command could be seen. All the generals, who had been strolling about quite proudly in their gold uniforms, bustled and, with low bows, seemed to catch his every word and even his slightest movement, ready to fly at once to carry it out. But the hetman did not even pay attention, barely nodded his head and went up to the Zaporozhians.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Zaporozhians all bowed to his feet.

speaker: POTEMKIN
text: “Are you all here?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he asked, drawling, pronouncing the words a little through his nose.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “All here, father!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the Zaporozhians, bowing again.

speaker: POTEMKIN
text: “You will not forget to speak as I taught you?”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “No, father, we will not forget.”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Is that the Tsar?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith asked one of the Zaporozhians.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “The Tsar, indeed! That is Potemkin himself,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the man.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Voices were heard in another room, and the blacksmith did not know where to put his eyes at the multitude of ladies who came in, in satin dresses with long trains, and courtiers in gold-embroidered coats with bunches of hair at the back. He saw only glitter and nothing more. The Zaporozhians suddenly all fell to the ground and cried with one voice:

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Have mercy, Mother! Have mercy!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith, seeing nothing, stretched himself out on the floor too, with all diligence.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “Rise!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: a commanding and at the same time pleasant voice sounded above them. Some of the courtiers bustled and nudged the Zaporozhians.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “We will not rise, Mother! We will not rise! We will die, but we will not rise!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the Zaporozhians.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Potemkin bit his lips; at last he came up himself and whispered a command to one of the Zaporozhians. The Zaporozhians rose.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then the blacksmith too dared to raise his head and saw standing before him a woman of small height, even somewhat stout, powdered, with blue eyes and at the same time a majestically smiling air which knew how to subdue everyone and could belong only to a reigning woman.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “His Serene Highness promised to acquaint me today with my people, whom I have never yet seen,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the lady with the blue eyes, examining the Zaporozhians with curiosity.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “Are you well kept here?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: she went on, coming nearer.

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Thank you, Mother! They give good provisions, though the sheep here are quite unlike ours in Zaporozhia; but why not live somehow?...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Potemkin frowned, seeing that the Zaporozhians were saying quite the opposite of what he had taught them...

speaker: NARRATOR
text: One of the Zaporozhians, drawing himself up, stepped forward:

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Have mercy, Mother! How has Thy faithful people angered Thee? Did we hold the hand of the filthy Tatar? Did we agree in anything with the Turk? Have we betrayed Thee in deed or in thought? Why then this displeasure? Before, we heard that Thou orderest fortresses to be built everywhere against us; later we heard that Thou wishest to turn us into carabineers; now we hear of new misfortunes. What is the fault of the Zaporozhian Host? That it took Thy army across Perekop and helped Thy generals cut down the Crimeans?...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Potemkin was silent and carelessly cleaned with a small brush the diamonds with which his hands were studded.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “What is it that you want?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Catherine asked with concern.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Zaporozhians looked meaningfully at each other.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Now is the time! The Empress asks what you want!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the blacksmith said to himself and suddenly threw himself on the ground:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Your Imperial Majesty, do not order me executed, order me pardoned! What, no offence meant to Your Imperial mercy, are the little shoes on Your feet made of? I think no cobbler in any kingdom in the world could make them so. My God, what if my wife wore such shoes!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Empress laughed. The courtiers laughed too. Potemkin both frowned and smiled. The Zaporozhians began to nudge the blacksmith's arm, wondering whether he had gone mad.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “Rise!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Empress kindly.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “If you want so much to have such shoes, it is not hard to do. Bring him at once the dearest shoes, with gold! Truly, I like this simplicity very much! Here,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the Empress went on, fixing her eyes on a middle-aged man standing apart from the others, with a full but somewhat pale face, whose modest coat with large mother-of-pearl buttons showed that he did not belong to the courtiers,

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “is a subject worthy of your witty pen!”

speaker: WRITER
text: “Your Imperial Majesty is too gracious. For this one would need at least a La Fontaine!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the man with the pearl buttons, bowing.

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “Upon my honour I tell you: I am still beside myself over your 'Brigadier'. You read wonderfully well! But,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the Empress went on, turning again to the Zaporozhians,

speaker: EMPRESS
text: “I have heard that in the Sich you never marry.”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “Why, Mother! Surely a man, as You Yourself know, cannot live without a wife,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the same Zaporozhian who had talked with the blacksmith, and the blacksmith was surprised to hear that this Zaporozhian, who knew the learned language so well, was speaking to the Empress, as if on purpose, in the coarsest dialect, usually called peasant speech.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “A cunning people!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he thought to himself.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Surely he does this for a reason.”

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “We are not monks,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the Zaporozhian went on,

speaker: ZAPOROZHIAN
text: “but sinful men. We are as prone, like all honest Christendom, to forbidden food. There are not a few among us who have wives, only they do not live with them in the Sich. There are some who have wives in Poland; there are some who have wives in Ukraine; there are some who have wives in Turkey too.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: At this time the shoes were brought to the blacksmith.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “My God, what an ornament!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he cried joyfully, seizing the shoes.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Your Imperial Majesty! If shoes like these are on Your feet, and in them, most likely, Your Honour goes skating on the ice, what must the feet themselves be? I think, at the very least, of pure sugar.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The Empress, who truly had the most shapely and charming feet, could not help smiling at hearing such a compliment from the lips of the simple blacksmith, who in his Zaporozhian dress might have passed for a handsome man, in spite of his dark face.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Delighted by such gracious attention, the blacksmith was about to question the Empress closely about everything: whether it is true that tsars eat nothing but honey and lard, and the like; but feeling the Zaporozhians nudge him in the ribs, he decided to be silent; and when the Empress, turning to the old men, began to ask how they lived in the Sich and what customs they had, he stepped back, bent to his pocket, said quietly:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Carry me out of here quickly!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and suddenly found himself beyond the barrier.

speaker: WEAVER_WIFE
text: “Drowned! By God, drowned! May I not move from this spot if he did not drown!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: babbled the stout weaver's wife, standing in a knot of Dikanka women in the middle of the street.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “What, am I some kind of liar? Have I stolen someone's cow? Have I put the evil eye on someone, that I am not believed?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried a woman in a Cossack coat with a violet nose, waving her hands.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “May I never want to drink water again if old Pereperchikha did not see with her own eyes how the blacksmith hanged himself!”

speaker: HEAD
text: “The blacksmith hanged himself? Well, there you are!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the Headman, who was coming out from Chub's; he stopped and pushed his way closer to those who were talking.

speaker: WEAVER_WIFE
text: “Say rather may you never want to drink vodka, you old drunkard!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: answered the weaver's wife.

speaker: WEAVER_WIFE
text: “One would have to be as mad as you to hang oneself! He drowned! Drowned in an ice-hole! I know that as surely as that you were at the tavern-keeper's just now.”

speaker: WOMAN
text: “Shameless creature! Look what she is reproaching me with!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: retorted the woman with the violet nose angrily.

speaker: WOMAN
text: “Be quiet, you worthless thing! Don't I know that the deacon comes to you every evening?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The weaver's wife flared up.

speaker: WEAVER_WIFE
text: “What deacon? Who is the deacon coming to? What are you lying about?”

speaker: DEACON_WIFE
text: “The deacon?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: sang out the deacon's wife, pressing toward the disputants, in a hareskin coat covered with blue Chinese cotton.

speaker: DEACON_WIFE
text: “I will give you a deacon! Who is saying deacon?”

speaker: WOMAN
text: “There, that is who the deacon visits!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the woman with the violet nose, pointing to the weaver's wife.

speaker: DEACON_WIFE
text: “So it is you, bitch,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the deacon's wife, advancing on the weaver's wife,

speaker: DEACON_WIFE
text: “so it is you, witch, who cast a fog on him and give him unclean potions to drink, so that he will come to you!”

speaker: WEAVER_WIFE
text: “Leave me alone, Satan!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the weaver's wife, backing away.

speaker: DEACON_WIFE
text: “Look at her, the accursed witch, may you never live to see your children, you worthless creature! Phew!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here the deacon's wife spat right in the weaver's wife's eyes.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The weaver's wife wanted to do the same, but instead spat into the unshaven beard of the Headman, who, the better to hear everything, had worked his way up to the very disputants.

speaker: HEAD
text: “Ah, foul woman!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried the Headman, wiping his face with the skirt of his coat and raising his whip. This movement made everyone scatter, swearing, in different directions.

speaker: HEAD
text: “What filth!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he kept repeating, still wiping himself.

speaker: HEAD
text: “So the blacksmith has drowned! My God, and what a fine painter he was! What strong knives, sickles and ploughs he knew how to forge! What strength he had! Yes,”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he went on, thinking,

speaker: HEAD
text: “there are few such men in our village. That is why, while still sitting in the accursed sack, I noticed that the poor fellow was in a very bad mood. So much for the blacksmith! He was, and now he is no more! And I was just about to have my dappled mare shod!...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And, full of such Christian thoughts, the Headman slowly trudged to his cottage.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Oksana was confused when such news reached her. She put little faith in Pereperchikha's eyes and the women's talk: she knew that the blacksmith was pious enough not to decide to destroy his soul. But what if he really had gone away with the intention of never returning to the village? And it is doubtful whether another such fine fellow as the blacksmith could be found anywhere! And he had loved her so! He had endured her whims longer than anyone! All night, under her blanket, the beauty turned from her right side to her left, from her left to her right, and could not sleep. Now, tossing in a bewitching nakedness which the darkness of night hid even from herself, she almost aloud scolded herself; now, growing quiet, she resolved to think of nothing, and kept thinking. And she was all aflame; and by morning she was head over heels in love with the blacksmith.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub showed neither joy nor sorrow at Vakula's fate. His thoughts were occupied with one thing: he could not forget Solokha's treachery, and even asleep he did not cease to curse her.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Morning came. The whole church was full of people even before daylight. Elderly women in white head-cloths, in white cloth coats, crossed themselves piously at the very entrance of the church. Gentlewomen in green and yellow jackets, and some even in blue kuntushes with gold whiskers behind, stood in front of them. Girls with a whole shop of ribbons wound on their heads, and on their necks strings of beads, crosses and ducats, tried to push in still nearer to the iconostasis. But in front of all stood the gentlemen and plain peasants with moustaches, with forelocks, with thick necks and chins just shaved, mostly in cloaks, from under which a white, or on some a blue, coat was showing. On all faces, wherever you looked, the holiday could be seen: the Headman licked his lips, imagining how he would break his fast with sausage; the girls were thinking how they would skate on the ice with the lads; the old women whispered their prayers more zealously than ever.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: All over the church one could hear how the Cossack Svyerbyhuz made his bows. Only Oksana stood as if not herself. She prayed and did not pray. In her heart so many different feelings were crowded, one more vexing than another, one sadder than another, that her face expressed only strong confusion; tears trembled in her eyes. The girls could not understand the cause and did not suspect that the blacksmith was to blame. Yet Oksana was not the only one occupied with the blacksmith. All the villagers noticed that the holiday was somehow not a holiday; that something was somehow missing. As bad luck would have it, the deacon, after his journey in the sack, was hoarse and quavered in a barely audible voice; true, the visiting singer took the bass splendidly, but how much better if the blacksmith had been there, who always, as soon as they sang Our Father or Who the Cherubim, used to go up to the choir and lead from there in the same tune as they sing in Poltava. Besides, he alone performed the duties of church warden. Already morning service was over; after morning service, the liturgy was over... where, indeed, had the blacksmith got to?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Still faster through the rest of the night the devil sped back with the blacksmith. And in a moment Vakula found himself beside his cottage. At that moment a cock crowed.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Where to?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: he cried, seizing by the tail the devil who wanted to run away.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Wait, my friend, not everything yet: I have not yet thanked you.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then, seizing a switch, he gave him three blows, and the poor devil took to his heels like a peasant who has just been flogged by the assessor. So, instead of leading astray, tempting and making fools of others, the enemy of mankind was himself made a fool of.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: After this Vakula went into the porch, burrowed into the hay and slept till noon. Waking, he was frightened when he saw that the sun was already high:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “I have slept through morning service and the liturgy!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The pious blacksmith sank into dejection, reasoning that surely God had purposely, as a punishment for his sinful intention of destroying his soul, sent him a sleep that did not even let him be in church on such a solemn holiday. But, comforting himself that next week he would confess this to the priest, and from today would begin to make fifty prostrations every day for a whole year, he looked into the cottage; but no one was in it. Evidently Solokha had not yet returned. Carefully he took the shoes from his bosom and again marvelled at the costly work and the wonderful adventure of the past night; he washed, dressed as well as he could, put on the very clothes which he had got from the Zaporozhians, took from the chest a new cap of Reshetilovka lambskin with a blue top, which he had not worn once since buying it back in Poltava; he also took a new belt of all colours; he put all this together with a whip in a kerchief and set off straight for Chub's.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub goggled when the blacksmith came in to him, and did not know what to wonder at: whether that the blacksmith had risen from the dead, or that the blacksmith dared to come to him, or that he had dressed up as such a dandy and a Zaporozhian. But he was still more astonished when Vakula untied the kerchief and laid before him a brand-new cap and a belt such as had never been seen in the village, and himself fell at his feet and said in a pleading voice:

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Have mercy, father! Do not be angry! Here is a whip for you: beat me as much as your heart desires, I give myself up; I repent of everything; beat me, only do not be angry! You once were brothers in arms with my late father, ate bread and salt together and drank to the bargain.”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Not without secret pleasure Chub saw the blacksmith, who feared no one in the village and bent coins and horseshoes in his hand like buckwheat pancakes, lying at his feet. So as not to lower himself further, Chub took the whip and struck him three times on the back.

speaker: CHUB
text: “Well, that is enough for you, get up! Always listen to old people! Let us forget all that was between us! Now say, what do you want?”

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Give Oksana to me, father!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Chub thought a little, looked at the cap and belt, the cap was a wonder, the belt was not inferior to it, remembered treacherous Solokha, and said resolutely:

speaker: CHUB
text: “Good! Send the matchmakers!”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “Ah!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: cried Oksana, stepping over the threshold and seeing the blacksmith, and fixed her eyes on him with amazement and joy.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “Look what shoes I have brought you!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said Vakula.

speaker: VAKULA
text: “The very ones the Empress wears.”

speaker: OKSANA
text: “No! No! I don't need shoes!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: she said, waving her hands and not taking her eyes from him.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “I will, even without shoes...”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: She did not finish and blushed.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The blacksmith came nearer and took her hand; the beauty lowered her eyes. Never before had she been so wonderfully pretty. The delighted blacksmith kissed her softly, and her face flamed more and she became lovelier still.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: A bishop of blessed memory passed through Dikanka, praised the place where the village stands, and, driving along the street, stopped before a new cottage.

speaker: BISHOP
text: “And whose is this painted cottage?”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: the bishop asked a handsome woman with a child in her arms, who was standing near the door.

speaker: OKSANA
text: “The blacksmith Vakula's!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Oksana said to him, bowing, because it was she.

speaker: BISHOP
text: “Splendid! Splendid work!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: said the bishop, examining the doors and windows. And the windows were all outlined round with red paint; and on the doors everywhere were Cossacks on horses with pipes in their teeth. But the bishop praised Vakula still more when he learned that he had served the church penance and had painted the whole left choir for nothing, with green paint and red flowers. And that is not all: on the wall at the side, as you enter the church, Vakula painted the devil in hell, so ugly that everyone spat when they passed by; and the women, as soon as a child began to cry in their arms, would bring it to the picture and say:

speaker: WOMAN
text: “Look, see what an ugly thing is painted!”

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and the child, holding back its little tears, squinted at the picture and pressed to its mother's breast.
